blindSummary:
This country is one of the most socially accepting destinations in its region for trans visitors, with deep cultural traditions of gender diversity (long-standing local identities spanning feminine and masculine presentation), a vibrant Pride scene in the capital, and no criminalisation — trans identity has never been criminalised.

However, there is a near-complete absence of legal protection at the national level: no legal gender recognition law at all (trans people cannot change their gender marker), the equality bill covering sexual orientation and gender identity has been stalled for 25 years (no national anti-discrimination law), and documented violence includes the killing of an 18-year-old trans woman found in a river days after going missing (June 2025), a foreign national arrested for raping a trans woman at a resort (May 2025), and a drag artist assaulted mid-performance. The national human-rights commission actively investigates discrimination cases but lacks enforcement power without a national law.

For a visitor: no border friction, social acceptance is genuine, but the legal-protection vacuum means limited recourse if discriminated against at a venue (documented incidents of bathroom, fitting-room, and resort denials).
blindOutOfScope: General crime (kidnapping risks in certain states/provinces, scams, severe-storm risk) affects all travellers; only trans-specific risk is assessed here.
blindSourceSummaries: International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): this country is consistently placed among its region's most 'accepting' countries toward LGBTIQ persons; but only 22% of the public supported same-sex civil unions (a 2018 national survey) and a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets; executive orders in 2019 and 2023 institutionalised and strengthened a national diversity-and-inclusion programme; no legal gender recognition.

News outlet (June 2025): the killing of an 18-year-old trans woman, found in a river days after going missing, prompts groups to push for the equality bill covering sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics; an LGBT alliance calls it another harrowing case in a series of recent trans killings.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying national-newspaper report (May 2025) covers a foreigner arrested for raping a trans woman in a provincial area.
LGBT media outlet (April 2024): the assault on a drag artist mid-performance in a provincial town sparks renewed push for the equality bill; the artist described the incident as traumatic.

International culture magazine's local edition, an explainer on the laws LGBTQ+ people here need to know: overview of the few protective laws and the gaps (no national anti-discrimination law, no marriage equality).
Independent news site: transgender people here demand legal gender recognition - advocacy for the right to change identity documents.

Travel-safety platform page on the capital (2026): safety confidence scores (LGBTQ+ 69 'Generally Safe', trans 62 'Exercise Caution'); strong social acceptance and cultural visibility (long-standing indigenous gender-variance identities, vibrant Pride) coexist with a near-complete absence of national legal protections; the equality bill (filed 2000) remains stuck in the national legislature.

NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 404); the underlying national human-rights commission statement addressed a viral video allegedly showing a trans woman compelled to get a haircut as a condition for school enrollment in the capital.

International human-rights organisation report (June 2017) on discrimination against LGBT students in this country: bullying and exclusion in schools; it opens with an 18-year-old student recalling that a legislator and former world-champion boxer had said people like them 'are not human' - 'they should just be left alone'; the law provides protections but implementation is lacking.
blindLocalsOnly: The absent legal-gender-recognition law, the 25-year-stalled equality bill, and the human-rights commission's lack of enforcement power are resident-facing; the 2025 killings affect residents primarily.
